h1: The 5 Best 1000-Watt Microwaves of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: five 1000-watt microwaves from Toshiba, Sharp, GE and BLACK+DECKER, covering countertop and over-the-range picks by size.
summary: The TOSHIBA 1.2 cu ft countertop is the best 1000W microwave for most kitchens because it combines a roomy cavity with no installation. The Smart Sensor version adds a sensor feature at the same size and bucket, and the Sharp SMC1162KS suits stainless kitchens with less counter room. The GE and BLACK+DECKER over-the-range models free the counter, with the GE listing a 300 CFM vent.
intro: Wattage is the number everyone shops by, and at 1000W it stops being a differentiator. Every microwave in this guide cooks at the same power, so the real decisions are physical: how big the cavity is, whether the box sits on a counter or bolts above the stove, and whether it doubles as a range hood. Get those wrong and the wattage is irrelevant.

We reviewed five 1000W microwaves and scored them on the Primea framework, weighing cavity size, mounting style, listed features and price bucket. Listings were thin on details such as turntable size and control layouts, so where data is missing we say so rather than guess. Measure your counter or range opening before you click buy, and note the door swing too.

products.name: TOSHIBA Countertop Microwave Oven
products.verdict: A 1.2 cu ft, 1000W countertop with no drama.
products.description:
The TOSHIBA countertop microwave pairs a 1.2 cu ft cavity with 1000W, in the $100 to $200 bucket. A 1.2 cu ft cavity is large enough for a full dinner plate and a tall mug at once, which is where smaller countertop units start to make you rearrange the load. At 1000W, reheating a plate takes noticeably less time than on lower-power boxes.

It ranks first because it combines a roomy cavity with a countertop footprint, without the install work of an over-the-range model. Against the Sharp below it offers more capacity, at the cost of more counter space.

Buy it for a family that wants a straightforward, large microwave. The caveat is that the listing names few features, and it needs counter room, so skip it if your counter is short of space.
products.idealFor: Families wanting a roomy countertop microwave.

products.name: TOSHIBA Countertop Microwave Oven with Smart Sensor
products.verdict: Same size and power as the top pick, plus a sensor.
products.description:
The TOSHIBA with Smart Sensor is a 1.2 cu ft, 1000W countertop microwave in the $100 to $200 bucket, and the name highlights a sensor feature. Sensor cooking measures steam from the food and adjusts the time, which takes the guesswork out of reheating a plate or popping a bag of popcorn.

It ranks second only because the base Toshiba gives you the same capacity and power in the same bucket, so the sensor is the single reason to pay attention to this one. The listing does not describe how the sensor works, so the benefit is unproven on paper.

Buy it if you want sensor cooking in a standard-size countertop box. Skip it if you want the plainer model, since it shares the same footprint, cavity and power, and treat the sensor as a bonus and not a reason to spend more.
products.idealFor: Cooks who want sensor features at standard size.
products.skipIf: You just want the plainer, proven model.

products.name: Sharp SMC1162KS 1.1 cu. ft. 1000W Stainless Steel Countertop
products.verdict: Slightly smaller cavity, stainless finish, same 1000W.
products.description:
The Sharp SMC1162KS is a 1.1 cu ft, 1000W countertop microwave in a stainless steel finish, in the $100 to $200 bucket. Stainless matches modern appliance suites, and a slightly smaller body suits shorter counters better than a 1.2 cu ft Toshiba.

Third place comes down to the Toshibas offering 0.1 cu ft more room. The advantage here is a tidier footprint and the look. In practice, 0.1 cu ft changes whether a wide casserole dish fits, which is the sort of detail that decides daily use.

Buy it if you want a stainless unit for a modern kitchen. The caveat is the smaller interior, so skip it if you cook large dishes often, and note that the listing gives few feature details beyond power and finish.
products.idealFor: Kitchens with a stainless theme and limited counter room.

products.name: GE 30" Over-the-Range Microwave
products.verdict: Frees the counter and doubles as a range hood.
products.description:
The GE 30 inch Over-the-Range Microwave lists a 1.6 cu ft cavity, a 300 CFM hood vent and LED lighting, with 1000W of power, in the $200 to $500 bucket. An over-the-range model replaces your range hood, so it frees the counter and vents cooktop steam. The 300 CFM figure is the airflow its fan can move.

Fourth place reflects the install: it must mount above a range, and it costs more than the countertop picks. In return, it clears counter space and adds ventilation the others lack. Against the BLACK+DECKER, it gives up 0.1 cu ft of cavity but documents its vent and lighting.

Buy it when you are replacing a hood. The caveat is installation, so skip it if you have no wall space above the range or cannot mount a unit that heavy.
products.idealFor: Kitchens replacing a range hood with a microwave.
products.skipIf: You have no wall space above the range.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER Over the Range Microwave Oven
products.verdict: The largest cavity here, but it needs installing.
products.description:
The BLACK+DECKER Over the Range microwave offers a 1.7 cu ft cavity and 1000W, in the $200 to $500 bucket. At 1.7 cu ft, it is the largest interior here, which matters for big casseroles and large platters that a 1.1 cu ft box simply cannot take.

Last place goes here since the GE adds a listed 300 CFM vent and LED lighting, while this listing gives only capacity and power. An over-the-range unit that cannot state its vent airflow is a gamble for the buyer who plans to cook above it. It does win on interior size.

Buy it if you want the most space above the stove. The caveat is that vent specs are not listed, so confirm them with the seller. Skip it if you need to verify ventilation before buying.
products.idealFor: Big households replacing a range hood.

whatMatters.detail: Capacity is the interior volume in cubic feet. It matters because a 1.1 cu ft cavity handles fewer large plates and dishes than the 1.6 or 1.7 cu ft models. Check the cubic feet figure in the title, then think about the biggest dish you reheat, and whether a family-size plate fits flat inside. Turntable clearance matters as much as raw volume.

Mounting style is whether the microwave sits on a counter or mounts above the stove. Countertop units plug in anywhere, while over-the-range models often act as a hood. It matters because the wrong choice means no space or a failed install. Measure your counter width or range opening before buying, and check the listing for a mounting kit. A tight cabinet gap can rule out an over-the-range unit entirely.

Wattage is cooking power, and at 1000W food heats faster than on weaker models. All five picks list it, so it is a baseline, not a differentiator. Look for the number in the title, not a marketing phrase like powerful, and use it to rule out boxes that fall below the range you want. Compact models under 1000W take noticeably longer.

Ventilation matters on over-the-range models, which can include a hood fan measured in CFM. The fan handles cooktop steam, smoke and grease. Check for a listed CFM figure, such as the 300 CFM on the GE, and be cautious when a listing omits it, as the BLACK+DECKER does. A hood without an airflow figure is a gamble above a busy cooktop.

Price bucket shows what installation convenience costs. The five picks span $100 to $200 for countertop boxes up to $200 to $500 for over-the-range units. Decide whether you actually need the install and the hood before paying, because a countertop model does the same cooking for less money. Pay for the hood function only if you will use it.

faq.a: For most home cooking and reheating, yes. All five picks here list 1000W, so the choice comes down to cavity size and mounting, not power. A 1.2 cu ft Toshiba covers everyday needs, and anything bigger helps only with large dishes.

faq.q: What is the biggest buying mistake?
faq.a: Assuming wattage tells you about size. Measure your counter or range opening, with door clearance, before ordering, because a TOSHIBA at 1.2 cu ft and a GE over-the-range at 1.6 cu ft both list 1000W but need different spaces.

faq.q: Is the Smart Sensor Toshiba worth it?
faq.a: Only if you want sensor-assisted cooking. The base Toshiba matches it on capacity and power in the same bucket, so the sensor is the only reason to pick the second model.

Yes, they mount above the range. Plan for wall space and a compatible opening, and note that the GE and BLACK+DECKER both need installation, unlike the countertop TOSHIBA and Sharp. A cabinet above the range may limit what fits.

Wipe the interior after spills and keep vents clear. Follow the manual for filters on hood models like the GE, since a clogged hood filter hurts both cooking and ventilation. Counter models need only a wipe-down.

faq.q: Why is the LG not here?
faq.a: The LG's listing does not state 1000W, so it does not match the title. Every model here, from the TOSHIBA to the BLACK+DECKER, lists 1000W, which keeps the comparison honest.

finalTake: For most households, buy the TOSHIBA and keep it simple, adding the Smart Sensor version only if sensor cooking appeals. Choose the Sharp when counter space is tight. Over-the-range buyers should take the GE for its listed 300 CFM vent and LED lighting, and the BLACK+DECKER only if the 1.7 cu ft cavity matters more than confirmed ventilation. Measure first, because fit decides everything here.
